1149.title: The outcaste at Kashi
1149.hook: a great teacher tells a man to step aside, and Shiva answers with a question
1149.carry: shiva lives in everyone, so everyone gets the bow
1149.howItsDone: Chanters learn the Namakam's paired lines (namo jyeshthaya cha kanishthaya cha and others) by heart, usually from a teacher, and recite them in Vedic Sanskrit at home, in temples and in group chanting.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: namah, the bow leaves no one out, the Rudram's heartbeat, said again and again.
screen: `NAMAH — A BOW.` · `TODAY: WHO GETS THE BOW.`

segments.voice: Kashi, on the banks of the Ganga, early morning. The young teacher Shankara is walking up from his bath with his students when a man blocks the narrow lane, a man the town treated as an outcaste, with four dogs at his heels. The students call out: move aside. The man doesn't move. He asks a question instead. Which should step aside? This body from your body, both made of the same food? Or the Self in me from the Self in you, when it's the same Self? Shankara stops.
screen: `KASHI. A NARROW LANE.` → `MOVE ASIDE.` → `WHICH ONE OF ME SHOULD MOVE?`

segments.voice: Tradition says Shankara bowed to the man right there, and that the outcaste was Shiva himself, with the four Vedas as his dogs. The short poem Shankara is said to have made that morning, the Manisha Panchakam, says it plainly: whoever sees the one Self in all, brahmin or outcaste, is my teacher. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the same Lord lives in every being. The Rudram sings it in its own way. In one stretch of the Namakam, the bows come in pairs. A bow to the short one, and to the dwarf. To the large one, and to the one grown old. To the eldest, and to the youngest. To the firstborn, and to the one born after. To the middle one, and to the one not yet grown, still unsure of themselves. Rudra is all of them. Short and tall, first and last: the very measures people use to rank each other. The hymn doesn't erase the differences. It names every one, and gives every one the same small word, namah. Nobody's bow is louder. Many teachers read the folded hands of namaste the same way: a bow to the divine in the person in front of you. In a Hindu home, children still touch their elders' feet, and that respect is real. But the bow itself, in the Rudram, goes to every rung, down to the shy kid at the end of the table.
screen: `SHIVA, AS THE OUTCASTE.` · `THE SAME LORD IN EVERY BEING.` · `THE ELDEST, THE YOUNGEST, THE SHY ONE.` · `THE SAME BOW FOR EVERY RUNG.` · then, large: `NOBODY'S NAMAH IS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people in your family, or the family you've made, from the eldest you can think of down to the youngest, and give each one a breath and the same inward bow, hands folded at the heart if you like, the way you'd say namaste. If one is harder to bow to, stay a little longer with that one. If you pray, you can say namah shivaya for each of them; if you don't, the quiet bow is enough.
The Rudram. Today's lines: a bow to the eldest and the youngest, the firstborn and the later-born, the middle one and the shy one. And the outcaste in the lane at Kashi, who was Shiva.
screen: `THE RUDRAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Shiva lives in everyone, so everyone gets the bow. Even the one you'd ask to step aside. Go gently.

1150.howItsDone: The Rudram's lines about trees, rain and water are chanted in Vedic Sanskrit as part of the whole Namakam, often during abhishekam in Shiva temples. Ganga water is poured over the linga, and in the month of Shravan pilgrims called kanwariyas carry it on foot to Shiva temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shiva lives in everyone, so everyone gets the bow. The Rudram bowed to a whole family, and Shiva stood in a lane at Kashi as an outcaste.
screen: `THE ELDEST AND THE YOUNGEST.` · `TODAY: THE LAND AND THE SKY.`

segments.voice: A king named Bhagiratha has one wish: bring the river Ganga down from heaven, so her water can reach the ashes of his ancestors and set them free. After long austerities, he's granted it. But there's a problem. Ganga is a goddess, and proud, and a river falling from the sky would smash the earth. Only one god can take that weight. So Bhagiratha turns to Shiva, and Shiva stands under the falling sky and opens his matted hair.
screen: `A KING ASKS FOR A RIVER.` → `IT WOULD SMASH THE EARTH.` → `SHIVA OPENS HIS HAIR.`

segments.voice: In the Ramayana's telling, Ganga crashes into his locks and is lost there, wandering in his hair, until Shiva lets her out gently, in streams. The wild water becomes a river that feeds a whole land. That's why Shiva is pictured with Ganga in his hair. And it's why Ganga water is poured over Shiva's linga: in the month of Shravan, pilgrims carry it on foot, sometimes for days, to pour on him. Behind the story is a big Hindu teaching: God isn't only above nature, God is in it, the gentle and the fierce alike. The Rudram said it long before. A bow to the trees, the green-haired ones: Rudra in the trees, with leaves for hair. A bow to the one in the clouds, and to the one in the lightning. To the one in the rain, and to the one where no rain falls. To the one in wells, and in the young grass, and in the foam. Rain and no rain: the second half is the surprise. It's easy to thank God for the rain that feeds the crops. It's harder to bow in a drought. The Rudram does both, with the same word, because nothing is outside Rudra. Many teachers read Ganga's fall the same way: the force that could flatten the earth and the river that feeds it pass through the same hair. That's why, in Hindu eyes, a river can be a goddess and a tree can be holy ground.
screen: `GANGA IN SHIVA'S HAIR.` · `GOD IN NATURE, GENTLE AND FIERCE.` · `RAIN, AND NO RAIN.` · `NOTHING OUTSIDE RUDRA.` · then, large: `A RIVER CAN BE A GODDESS.`

segments.voice: Notice what the weather is doing right now, sun, cloud, rain, wind or still air, and pleasant or not, offer it a small inward bow. Then, if there's water nearby, pour a little slowly onto a plant or the ground, the way devotees pour Ganga water over the linga, and think of the river Shiva gentled. If you pray, say namah shivaya as you pour; if you don't, let the pour be your bow.
The Rudram. Today's lines: a bow to the green-haired trees, to cloud and lightning, to rain and to drought. And Ganga, caught in Shiva's hair.

1151.title: Upamanyu asks Shiva for milk
1151.hook: a hungry boy asks Shiva for milk, and the Rudram's companion asks for rice and lentils
1151.carry: asking shiva for ordinary needs is devotion too
1151.tomorrow: Why Hindus bathe the Shiva linga
1151.howItsDone: When the Shri Rudram is chanted in full, tradition pairs the Namakam with the Chamakam, and both are recited in Vedic Sanskrit, at home, in temples and during abhishekam.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: rain or drought, nothing is outside Shiva. The Rudram went outdoors: green-haired trees, and Ganga caught in Shiva's hair.
screen: `RAIN, AND NO RAIN.` · `TODAY: THE OTHER HALF.`

segments.voice: A small boy named Upamanyu, from a poor family of forest hermits, sees another child drinking milk, and runs home to ask for some. His mother has none. So she stirs a little flour into water and hands it to him. He takes one sip and knows. This isn't milk. And his mother, in the Mahabharata's telling, says the honest thing: people like us only get milk by Shiva's grace. So the boy decides to ask Shiva himself.
screen: `A BOY WANTS MILK.` → `FLOUR IN WATER.` → `ASK SHIVA HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: He goes to the mountains and prays with his whole small body. A god appears, looking like Indra on his great elephant, and offers him anything at all, if he'll stop asking Shiva. Upamanyu says no: from Shiva, or from no one. Then the disguise falls away. It was Shiva, testing him, and Shiva gives him milk without end, and something better, a devotion that never leaves him. Notice what the boy asked for. Not freedom from the world. Milk. And Shiva didn't scold him. This is a real Hindu teaching: asking God for ordinary needs is part of devotion, not beneath it. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names four kinds of people who come to him, among them the one in trouble and the one who wants something in this world, and he calls all of them good. The Rudram has a companion that says it in a list. When it's chanted in full, the bowing half, the Namakam, is paired with the Chamakam, where line after line ends in two small words: cha me, and to me. Strength, and to me. Ease, and what is dear. Milk and ghee and honey. Rice and barley, beans and sesame, wheat and lentils. Plowing, and rain. And eating together, and drinking together. Many teachers hear the pair like breathing. The Namakam breathes out: everything is Rudra's. The Chamakam breathes in: from all that, may this come to me.
screen: `FROM SHIVA, OR FROM NO ONE.` · `ASKING IS PART OF DEVOTION.` · `CHA ME — AND TO ME.` · `RICE, LENTILS, RAIN, A SHARED MEAL.` · then, large: `BOWING OUT, ASKING IN.`

segments.voice: Without judging the list, let a few plain needs come up, not big wishes but ordinary things: sleep, a good meal, someone to eat it with, rain if your garden is dry. Name each one quietly and hold it out, the way the Chamakam does, then let the list go on the out-breath. If you pray, offer these needs to Shiva in your own words, the way Upamanyu asked for milk; if you don't, just name them honestly.
The Rudram. Today, its companion, the Chamakam: cha me, and to me, asking plainly for grain, rain, and company at the table.
screen: `THE RUDRAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: asking Shiva for ordinary needs is devotion too. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.

1152.title: Why Hindus bathe the Shiva linga
1152.hook: Shiva drinks the world's poison, and devotees pour cool water over his linga
1152.carry: abhisheka cools the one who drank the poison
1152.tomorrow: The pillar of fire with no end
1152.howItsDone: In Shiva temples and in homes, Hindus may chant the Rudram during abhisheka, pouring water, milk and other offerings over the linga; some families arrange a Rudrabhisheka for a festival, a new home, or a hard time.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: asking Shiva for ordinary needs is devotion too. The Rudram's companion asked: cha me, and to me, right down to grain and a shared meal. Today is the last day inside the hymn.
screen: `ASKING IS DEVOTION TOO.` · `LAST DAY INSIDE THE HYMN.`

segments.voice: The gods and the demons are churning the ocean of milk, pulling a great serpent back and forth around a mountain, hoping to bring up the nectar of immortality. Before any treasure, something else comes up: a poison so strong its fumes start to burn the worlds. Everyone runs. Everyone goes to Shiva. And Shiva gathers the poison in his palm and drinks it. He holds it in his throat, where it stays, and his throat turns blue. That's why one of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated one.
screen: `THE OCEAN IS CHURNED.` → `A POISON THAT BURNS THE WORLDS.` → `SHIVA DRINKS IT.`

segments.voice: Now walk into a Shiva temple. Above the stone linga hangs a small pot with a pinhole in its base, and water drips onto the stone, one drop and then the next. On festival days priests sit close and pour water and milk over the linga while they chant. The bath is called abhisheka, and when the Rudram is chanted with it, people call the rite Rudrabhisheka. Why bathe this god? An old saying puts it simply: Vishnu loves to be adorned, Shiva loves to be bathed. And many devotees tie it to the churning: the one who swallowed the world's poison, with fire in his third eye, is offered coolness, again and again. Hold the hymn next to the water and it makes the same movement. It opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, his arrow and his bow, and asks that the bow be unstrung. Deep inside comes the line namah shivaya cha shivataraya cha: a bow to the kind one, and to the one kinder still. A traditional saying calls the Rudram the heart of the Vedas, namah shivaya the heart of the Rudram, and shi-va the heart of those five syllables. Take it as a picture, not a measurement. That's the teaching of the bath: Shiva took in the world's poison so others wouldn't have to, and devotees answer with water and a bow, one drop at a time, until the fierce one shows his kind face.
screen: `ABHISHEKA: THE SACRED BATH.` · `SHIVA LOVES TO BE BATHED.` · `COOLNESS FOR THE BLUE THROAT.` · `TO THE KIND ONE, AND KINDER STILL.` · then, large: `ONE DROP AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that feels like poison right now, a worry, a hard word, a deadline with its bow drawn, and without fighting or fixing it, picture cool water poured slowly over it on each out-breath, the way the priests pour over the linga. Let the thing stay what it is, and just keep pouring. If you pray, you can say namah shivaya softly with each pour, or the name of God you use; if you don't, let each out-breath be the pour.
The Rudram. A Vedic hymn that bows to the fierce Rudra until Shiva, the kind one, appears at its heart. Today, chanted as water pours over the linga of the blue-throated one.
screen: `THE RUDRAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: abhisheka cools the one who drank the poison. Tomorrow, a great night of Shiva. See you then.

segments.voice: Yesterday: abhisheka cools the one who drank the poison, the Rudram chanted as water poured over the linga. Now the night.
screen: `ABHISHEKA: WATER OVER STONE.` · `NOW THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Brahma and Vishnu are arguing about which of them is greatest, when a pillar of fire splits the dark between them. It has no top they can see, and no bottom. So they agree: whoever finds an end wins. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. They go for ages. Neither finds anything. And then Shiva steps out of the fire.
screen: `WHO IS GREATEST?` → `A PILLAR OF FIRE, NO END.` → `SHIVA STEPS OUT.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana's telling, the pillar of light is Shiva himself, without beginning or end, and the stone linga in every Shiva temple remembers it. Many Hindus tell this as the story of tonight's festival, and in many South Indian temples the middle of the night of Shivaratri is kept as the hour the pillar appeared. The name says it plainly. Maha, great. Shiva. Ratri, night. It falls in the dark half of the lunar month, the night before the new moon, when there's almost no moon to see by. The Shiva Purana describes the vow for it. Fast through the day. Worship Shiva in the linga, with water and bilva leaves. Stay awake until morning. Notice what kind of teaching this is. Nobody hands you a lecture. The night teaches through the body: hunger, sleepiness and the dark each take away something you usually lean on, and ask what's left. Brahma and Vishnu tried to measure Shiva and couldn't. On Shivaratri, people stop measuring and simply stay awake beside him. Some keep every hour in a crowded temple until sunrise. Some keep part of the night at home. The days ahead take it in order: the vow, the fast, keeping awake, the name, the offerings, and dawn.
screen: `THE PILLAR IS SHIVA, WITHOUT END.` · `MAHA, SHIVA, RATRI.` · `FAST, WORSHIP, STAY AWAKE.` · `THE NIGHT TEACHES THROUGH THE BODY.` · then, large: `STOP MEASURING. STAY AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Dim the light around you if you can, or simply close your eyes, and notice what the dark takes away, the screen, the faces, and what it gives back: sounds you hadn't heard, the weight of your body, the breath. Keep your attention on one thing, and come back to it whenever you drift. If you pray, let that one thing be Shiva's name, om namah shivaya, or the name of God you use; if you don't, the breath is enough.
Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva. Today, its story: the pillar of fire with no end. And its shape: a fast, worship, and staying awake until dawn.

segments.voice: Your line: Shivaratri is a night awake for the god without end. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1154.title: Parvati's vow and the sankalpa
1154.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1154.hook: Parvati makes a vow to win Shiva and keeps it, and the night of Shiva begins with a resolve said in daylight
1154.carry: a sankalpa: the vow said in daylight, kept in the dark
1154.howItsDone: Hindus keeping Maha Shivaratri may begin the day with a bath and a sankalpa, stating their intention to keep the fast and the vigil; a priest may lead the sankalpa before a temple puja.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maha Shivaratri as a night awake for the god without end, beside the pillar of fire. Today, the vow that begins it.
screen: `A NIGHT AWAKE.` · `TODAY: THE VOW.`

segments.voice: Long before she is Shiva's wife, Parvati is a young woman who has decided she will marry him. Shiva is deep in meditation and doesn't look up. So she makes a vow. She goes into the mountains and takes up austerity: she lives on fruit, then only leaves, then not even leaves. That's why one of her names is Aparna, the one without even a leaf. Then a young ascetic turns up and mocks her: why waste yourself on a wild god who lives in cremation grounds?
screen: `PARVATI MAKES A VOW.` → `FRUIT, THEN LEAVES, THEN NOTHING.` → `A STRANGER MOCKS IT.`

segments.voice: Parvati won't hear it. She turns to leave. And the young ascetic becomes Shiva. He was testing whether her vow would hold, and it did. That's why many Hindus, especially women, remember Parvati when they keep a fast to Shiva. Such a vow, a vrata, kept for a set time, traditionally starts the same way: with a sankalpa, a resolve made on purpose and said aloud. On the morning of Shivaratri, after a bath, someone keeping the night takes a little water into the right palm and says where they are, what day it is, who they are, and what they will do: I will keep this fast, I will keep this night. Then they let the water go. Why decide in the morning? Because the hours you'll need it are the hours you can't decide well. At two in the morning almost any reason to quit sounds wise. And water, once poured, can't be poured back. Behind it sits an old idea from the Chandogya Upanishad: a person is made of resolve, and what you resolve shapes what you become. A vow is also personal. Some fast completely. Some take fruit and milk. The vow that counts is the one you actually said, and kept, the way Parvati kept hers even while someone laughed.
screen: `APARNA: NOT EVEN A LEAF.` · `SANKALPA: A RESOLVE, SAID ALOUD.` · `DECIDE IN DAYLIGHT.` · `THE VOW YOU ACTUALLY SAID.` · then, large: `A PERSON IS MADE OF RESOLVE.`

segments.voice: Choose one small, honest thing you'll do before tomorrow, a meal eaten slowly or ten minutes without the phone, and say it quietly the way a sankalpa is said, with where you are and what day it is, a little water in your right palm if there's a glass nearby. Then let the water go, into a plant or a sink, and sit with what you've promised. If you pray, offer the resolve to Shiva and Parvati, or to the God you know; if you don't, the words and the water are enough.
Maha Shivaratri. Today: the sankalpa, the resolve made in the morning with water in the palm, and Parvati, who kept her vow.

1155.title: The hunter's accidental fast
1155.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1155.hook: a hungry hunter waits all night in a bilva tree, and his fast turns into worship
1155.carry: upavasa: the fast is staying near shiva
1155.tomorrow: The hunter in the bilva tree
1155.howItsDone: Hindus who fast on Maha Shivaratri keep different vows: some take only water, some take fruit, milk and special fasting foods such as sago, and the fast is usually broken the next morning after worship.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maha Shivaratri as a vow: a sankalpa said in daylight, kept in the dark, and Parvati, who kept hers. Today, the fast, and the week closes.
screen: `THE SANKALPA, MADE IN DAYLIGHT.` · `TODAY: THE FAST.`

segments.voice: A hunter goes into the forest on Shivaratri, though he has no idea it's Shivaratri. He hasn't eaten all day, and he's caught nothing. At dusk he climbs a bilva tree beside a pool, with a pot of water, to wait for animals coming to drink. He doesn't know there's a Shiva linga in the roots below him. Each time he shifts on the branch, a little water spills, and a few bilva leaves drift down onto the stone.
screen: `HUNGRY, IN A BILVA TREE.` → `WATER AND LEAVES FALL.` → `A LINGA BELOW, UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: He didn't choose to fast. He simply has nothing. But in the Shiva Purana's telling, that hungry night still counts: a fast, a night awake, water and bilva on the linga, all kept without knowing, and Shiva takes notice. The next days follow him through the night. Today, look at the empty stomach. Here's the teaching. The Sanskrit word for a fast is upavasa. Many teachers hear in it upa, near, and vasa, dwelling: staying near. A Hindu fast isn't mainly about going without. It's keeping close to the one the day is for. The hunter went hungry by accident, and his hunger kept him alert in a tree above a linga he couldn't even see. Families who fast on purpose turn that same hunger toward Shiva: each pang is a small reminder of whose day it is. And the fast sits inside a vow, not a punishment. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all. So families make room for children, the sick, and anyone a fast would hurt, and many keep a lighter vow of fruit and milk; a vow kept honestly is still the vow. Look back at the week: one bow for everyone, Ganga in Shiva's hair, a boy asking for milk, the poison and the bath, the endless pillar, Parvati's vow, and now a hungry hunter. Each time, something hard brings someone nearer to Shiva.
screen: `A HUNTER IN A BILVA TREE.` · `THE HUNGRY NIGHT STILL COUNTS.` · `UPAVASA: STAYING NEAR.` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT NONE AT ALL.` · then, large: `THE FAST KEEPS YOU CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Sooner or later something will tug at you, an itch, a thought of food, the urge to check a message; don't act on it or fight it, just ask quietly, who am I staying near, and come back. Each tug is one more return. If you pray, let each return carry om namah shivaya, or the name of God you use; if you don't, let the breath be the place you stay near.
Maha Shivaratri. Today: upavasa, the fast, staying near, and a hungry hunter who kept it without knowing.
